Optimization in economics

Section titled “Optimization in economics”

A basic assumption in economics is that people and firms make the best choice they can under constraints. Every optimization problem has three parts: the objective function that is maximized or minimized, the variables that can be chosen, and the constraints.

WhoObjectiveChoice variablesConstraints
ConsumerMaximize utilityHow much of each of two goods to buyBudget
FirmMaximize profitOutputCost
InvestorMinimize varianceWeights of the assetsTarget return; weights add up to 1

The last row is the portfolio optimization of 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory (not yet published).

One variable: derivatives and margins

Section titled “One variable: derivatives and margins”

The derivative is the slope of the graph of a function. Think of climbing a hill: at the top, the ground is flat and the slope is 0. So a point x∗x^*x∗ where a function has an interior maximum or minimum satisfies the first-order condition:

f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*) = 0f′(x∗)=0

Whether a point with slope 0 is a hilltop or a valley floor is decided by the second-order condition: f′′(x∗)<0f''(x^*) < 0f′′(x∗)<0 means a maximum, and f′′(x∗)>0f''(x^*) > 0f′′(x∗)>0 means a minimum.

The two parts of cost. A firm’s total cost C(q)C(q)C(q) has two parts:

C(q)=F+VC(q)C(q) = F + VC(q)C(q)=F+VC(q)
  • The fixed cost FFF: the part that must be paid however much is produced, for example rent and equipment leases. It does not depend on output qqq.
  • The variable cost VC(q)VC(q)VC(q): the part that changes with output, for example materials and piece-rate wages.

A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever is decided later, is a sunk cost.

In economics, “marginal” means the derivative. The increase in revenue from selling one more unit is the marginal revenue (MR), and the increase in cost from producing one more unit is the marginal cost (MC):

MC=C′(q)MC = C'(q)MC=C′(q)

Example: profit maximization. The price is 40 dollars and the cost is C(q)=100+q2C(q) = 100 + q^2C(q)=100+q2, with F=100F = 100F=100 and VC(q)=q2VC(q) = q^2VC(q)=q2. Profit is

π(q)=40q−100−q2\pi(q) = 40q - 100 - q^2π(q)=40q−100−q2

The first-order condition is

π′(q)=40−2q=0⇒q∗=20\pi'(q) = 40 - 2q = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad q^* = 20π′(q)=40−2q=0⇒q∗=20

π′′(q)=−2<0\pi''(q) = -2 < 0π′′(q)=−2<0, so this is a maximum, and π∗=800−100−400=300\pi^* = 800 - 100 - 400 = 300π∗=800−100−400=300.

π′(q)=0\pi'(q) = 0π′(q)=0 is the same as MR−MC=0MR - MC = 0MR−MC=0. Choosing output to make profit as large as possible is profit maximization; at an interior optimum, MR=MCMR = MCMR=MC. The intuition: as long as one more unit brings in more revenue than it costs, the firm should produce more.

Several variables: partial derivatives

Section titled “Several variables: partial derivatives”

For a function of two variables f(x,y)f(x, y)f(x,y), the slope when xxx changes and yyy stays fixed is the partial derivative of fff with respect to xxx, written ∂f∂x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}∂x∂f​. Without constraints, all partial derivatives are 0 at an interior optimum.

Example:

f(x,y)=−x2−y2+2x+8yf(x, y) = -x^2 - y^2 + 2x + 8yf(x,y)=−x2−y2+2x+8y ∂f∂x=−2x+2=0,∂f∂y=−2y+8=0\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -2x + 2 = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -2y + 8 = 0∂x∂f​=−2x+2=0,∂y∂f​=−2y+8=0

This gives x=1x = 1x=1, y=4y = 4y=4 and f=17f = 17f=17.

With two variables, the second-order condition depends not only on the signs of fxxf_{xx}fxx​ and fyyf_{yy}fyy​ but also on the cross term fxyf_{xy}fxy​ (4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory (not yet published) covers the general method). When the cross term is 0, fxx<0f_{xx} < 0fxx​<0 and fyy<0f_{yy} < 0fyy​<0 mean a maximum.

Optimization with a constraint: substitution

Section titled “Optimization with a constraint: substitution”

A consumer’s utility is U=xyU = xyU=xy, the prices of the two goods are px=2p_x = 2px​=2 and py=4p_y = 4py​=4, and the budget is 100 dollars. Spending cannot exceed the budget; this is the budget constraint. When all the money is spent:

2x+4y=1002x + 4y = 1002x+4y=100

Substitute y=25−x2y = 25 - \frac{x}{2}y=25−2x​ into the utility:

U=x(25−x2)=25x−x22,U′=25−x=0U = x\left(25 - \frac{x}{2}\right) = 25x - \frac{x^2}{2}, \qquad U' = 25 - x = 0U=x(25−2x​)=25x−2x2​,U′=25−x=0

This gives x∗=25x^* = 25x∗=25, y∗=12.5y^* = 12.5y∗=12.5 and U∗=312.5U^* = 312.5U∗=312.5.

Substitution has limits: when the constraint is complicated, it is hard to solve for one variable and substitute it; and it does not show how much more utility one more dollar of budget would buy.

The optimum under a constraint: moving one dollar and tangency

Section titled “The optimum under a constraint: moving one dollar and tangency”

Stand at a point on the budget line. Spend 1 dollar less on yyy and 1 dollar more on xxx; total spending stays the same. 1 dollar buys 1px\frac{1}{p_x}px​1​ units of xxx, so xxx rises by 1px\frac{1}{p_x}px​1​ units and yyy falls by 1py\frac{1}{p_y}py​1​ units. With the marginal utilities MUx=∂U∂xMU_x = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}MUx​=∂x∂U​ and MUy=∂U∂yMU_y = \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}MUy​=∂y∂U​, utility changes by about

MUxpx−MUypy\frac{MU_x}{p_x} - \frac{MU_y}{p_y}px​MUx​​−py​MUy​​

If this is positive, moving money from yyy to xxx raises utility; if it is negative, moving money the other way does. So at an optimum inside the budget line, moving money cannot help:

MUxpx=MUypy\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \frac{MU_y}{p_y}px​MUx​​=py​MUy​​

Call this common value λ\lambdaλ.

Geometrically, at the optimum the utility contour is tangent to the budget line, and the gradients of the two curves (the directions perpendicular to them) are parallel. Write the budget as g(x,y)=pxx+pyyg(x, y) = p_x x + p_y yg(x,y)=px​x+py​y; then

∇U=λ ∇g\nabla U = \lambda\,\nabla g∇U=λ∇g

The Lagrange multiplier method

Section titled “The Lagrange multiplier method”

The condition from the previous section can be written as a fixed procedure. Form

L(x,y,λ)=xy+λ (100−2x−4y)\mathcal{L}(x, y, \lambda) = xy + \lambda\,(100 - 2x - 4y)L(x,y,λ)=xy+λ(100−2x−4y)

that is, the objective function plus λ\lambdaλ times (total resources − resources used). Here λ\lambdaλ is the Lagrange multiplier. Set the three partial derivatives to 0:

EquationMeaning
∂L∂x=y−2λ=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = y - 2\lambda = 0∂x∂L​=y−2λ=0, ∂L∂y=x−4λ=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y} = x - 4\lambda = 0∂y∂L​=x−4λ=0Moving money cannot help
∂L∂λ=100−2x−4y=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda} = 100 - 2x - 4y = 0∂λ∂L​=100−2x−4y=0On the budget line (the constraint itself)

Dividing the first two equations gives yx=12\frac{y}{x} = \frac{1}{2}xy​=21​, that is, x=2yx = 2yx=2y. Substituting into the constraint gives y∗=12.5y^* = 12.5y∗=12.5, x∗=25x^* = 25x∗=25 and λ=6.25\lambda = 6.25λ=6.25, the same as with substitution.

λ\lambdaλ has two meanings:

  • The equal-margin principle: MUxpx=MUypy=λ\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \frac{MU_y}{p_y} = \lambdapx​MUx​​=py​MUy​​=λ. The last dollar brings the same utility whichever good it is spent on.
  • When the constraint is relaxed by one unit (one more dollar of budget), the maximum utility rises by about λ\lambdaλ. This is the shadow price. It is an approximation: with a budget of 101, U∗≈318.78U^* \approx 318.78U∗≈318.78, about 6.28 more than 312.5, close to λ=6.25\lambda = 6.25λ=6.25.

Corner solutions and limits

Section titled “Corner solutions and limits”

The Lagrange solution always satisfies the equality constraint written into L\mathcal{L}L, but it does not guarantee x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, because those conditions are not written into it.

Example: U=ln⁡x+yU = \ln x + yU=lnx+y, px=1p_x = 1px​=1, py=10p_y = 10py​=10 and a budget of M=5M = 5M=5. The first-order conditions are 1x=λ\frac{1}{x} = \lambdax1​=λ and 1=10λ1 = 10\lambda1=10λ, which give λ=0.1\lambda = 0.1λ=0.1, x=10x = 10x=10 and y=5−1010=−0.5y = \frac{5 - 10}{10} = -0.5y=105−10​=−0.5. yyy is negative, which is not feasible.

The true optimum is to spend all the money on xxx: x=5x = 5x=5, y=0y = 0y=0. At this point MUxpx=1/51=0.2\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \frac{1/5}{1} = 0.2px​MUx​​=11/5​=0.2, which is more than MUypy=110=0.1\frac{MU_y}{p_y} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1py​MUy​​=101​=0.1. The consumer would like to move more money from yyy to xxx, but yyy is already 0. An optimum where a choice variable is at a boundary is a corner solution. At a corner, it is normal for the equal-margin condition not to hold.

Also, the budget constraint really says “spending is at most the budget”, but here it is treated as an equation. When more is always better, the optimum spends the whole budget, so this causes no problem. General inequality constraints need the KKT conditions (4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory (not yet published)).

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • An optimization problem = objective function + choice variables + constraints.
  • Without constraints: the first-order condition is that the derivative (or every partial derivative) is 0; the second-order condition separates maxima from minima.
  • Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost; marginal cost is the derivative of total cost. At an interior optimum of profit maximization, MR=MCMR = MCMR=MC.
  • With a constraint: at the optimum, moving one dollar cannot help; geometrically this is tangency, and algebraically it is the Lagrange condition. λ\lambdaλ is the shadow price (an approximation).
  • The Lagrange solution satisfies the equality constraint but may violate the non-negativity constraints; then the optimum is a corner solution.
